disputed.finding: The notes' claim that the 1977 law required 'semiannual consultations' and quote 'shall consult with Congress at semiannual hearings' is asserted in the memo with no visible quoted text; the draft should not repeat it without checking the Statutes at Large page.
disputed.objection: The notes expressly state the 1977 law required semiannual consultations and quote that language in the research memo, so this is not merely an unverified assertion in the notes.

disputed.finding: The quoted statutory sentence is described as the 'current' text in 12 U.S.C. § 225a; the notes only show the 1977 original and say the current text 'still contains the same opening sentence', and the draft offers no verification of the current wording.
disputed.objection: The notes say the current statute still contains the same opening sentence, so the finding that the draft offers no verification is unsupported by the notes themselves.

disputed.finding: Date of 'February 20 and July 20' reporting deadlines and 'Section 108' details come from the memo without visible excerpted text; the draft should not state them unless confirmed in the PL 95-523 text.
disputed.objection: The notes summarize the 1978 amendment details and dates in the memo, so the claim that they come from the memo without visible excerpted text is not something the notes establish as a problem.

disputed.finding: The claim that 'as of 2000 Congress struck the remaining report-to-Congress language' is not backed by anything in the notes beyond an unquoted U.S. Code note.
disputed.objection: The notes mention a later amendment note striking report language, so the finding that the claim is unbacked beyond an unquoted U.S. Code note is not settled by the notes.

disputed.finding: Humphrey-Hawkins is the popular name for the 1978 Act; the draft should note that naming, and that the act's reporting was later altered (Reports Elimination Act 2000), which the notes only weakly support.
disputed.objection: The notes do mention the 1978 act and report changes, but they do not settle whether the draft should specifically name Humphrey-Hawkins or the Reports Elimination Act of 2000.

disputed.finding: The draft says the mandate was established by the Federal Reserve Reform Act of 1977 (Public Law 95-188), enacted in 1977, which amended the Federal Reserve Act by adding Section 2A—now codified at 12 U.S.C. § 225a.[1][2] The notes support this, but the draft has not yet cited the official law title/date or a source for the codification note in the visible text; make sure the citations actually point to the session law and U.S. Code.
disputed.objection: The draft visibly cites [1][2] for this claim, and the notes' sources (the Statutes at Large PDF and uscode.house.gov) back it; asking for a 'law title/date' citation is a stylistic demand rather than a factual error.

disputed.finding: The draft begins quoting the statute but truncates it mid-sentence in the visible excerpt. If the full quote is not completed later, the claim about the full statutory wording is unsupported in the draft as shown.
disputed.objection: The truncation appears to be an artifact of the excerpt shown to the reviewer, and the notes contain the full sentence, so the claim is supported; it is speculative to treat it as unsupported.

disputed.finding: The draft may overstate the idea that the mandate is simply maximum employment and stable prices without explicitly distinguishing that from the statutory reference to moderate long-term interest rates. The notes say the Fed commonly treats that third item as part of the framework, not a separate practical objective.
disputed.objection: The draft already distinguishes the shorthand from the full statutory wording that includes moderate long-term interest rates, so the finding is a speculative overstatement.

omissions.point: The Fed calls it the 'dual mandate' because moderate long-term interest rates are treated as a result of achieving maximum employment and stable prices rather than a separate independent objective.
omissions.evidence: “the Fed’s mandate for monetary policy is commonly known as the dual mandate,”

omissions.point: The 2 percent PCE inflation goal is an FOMC policy choice, not statutory text, and the 1977 law already paired the goals with semiannual congressional consultations.
omissions.evidence: That makes the 2 percent PCE inflation goal a **Federal Reserve policy choice**, not a statutory number written into 12 U.S.C. § 225a.
